title: TWA Flight 800
one_line: A fuel tank explosion broke apart a Boeing 747 shortly after takeoff from New York.
status_why: Investigators established a fuel tank explosion and ruled out a missile or bomb. The exact ignition source remains unknown.

aircraft.livery_notes: FAA-hosted photograph identified as N93119 shows a light upper fuselage, red window-level striping, a red tail with white TWA lettering, and dark or bare-metal lower surfaces. Photograph date is not supplied. Exact paint state on 17 July 1996 is unverified. Dimensions are reference geometry; 6.5 m is maximum fuselage width rather than a truly circular diameter, and 19.58 m is the manufacturer's maximum ground tail height across loading/attitude conditions (s18).

site.description: Astronomical reference for the approximate accident site in s5: 40°40′N, 72°38′W; decimal conversion only, not an exact impact point. Wreckage fell across an area south of East Moriches. AAR p. 4 gives main wreckage bounds 40°37′42″–40°40′12″N, 72°40′48″–72°35′38″W. The nose and main body reached different places; a single exact impact coordinate is inappropriate.

terrain_box.why: Research framing choice, approximately 67 km east–west and 56 km north–south. Includes debris area, Moriches and Shinnecock inlets, coastal witness views and nearby airports. Include the low Long Island shoreline and Atlantic surface; this is coastal water rather than an isolated open-ocean scene.

environment.place: GOES-8 region within about 10 nm of accident site
environment.notes: s5 printed p. 6: infrared interpretation at 00:15 and 00:45 UTC placed local cloud tops below about 6,000 ft MSL. More developed cloud areas were about 30 nm northeast/southwest. Cloud types and local bases were not measured by this inference; do not equate it with Gabreski's separate 6,000 ft AGL layer. Radar at 00:27:35 and 00:33:25 showed weather echoes 50–55 km north/northeast. No significant accident-area weather identified.

A single-sensor transient was not corroborated or located. No convincing evidence of local electrical activity; lightning occurrence is therefore left null rather than claiming complete detection.

events.title: Previous flight lands
events.detail: The aircraft arrived at JFK from Athens as TWA flight 881 at about 16:31 EDT. Its incoming crew reported no operational abnormality.
events.caption: The aircraft arrived at JFK from Athens. Its incoming crew reported no operating problems.

events.title: Baggage concern resolved
events.detail: Gate staff advised that the passenger associated with a previously removed bag had been on board. Ground equipment and the baggage check had delayed departure.
events.locator: AAR section 1.1, pp. 1–2; official CVR transcript 1959:44
events.caption: Staff resolved a baggage concern that had delayed departure, confirming the passenger linked to the bag was aboard.

events.title: Crew requests pushback
events.detail: The crew requested pushback; physical pushback occurred about 20:02 EDT. Air-conditioning packs had operated on the ground before departure.
events.locator: CVR factual narrative printed p. 4; transcript 2001:42
events.caption: The crew requested pushback from the gate. The air conditioning had been running on the ground.

events.title: Crew requests taxi
events.detail: After starting engines 1, 2 and 4, the crew contacted ground control for taxi clearance.
events.caption: With three engines started, the crew requested clearance to taxi.

events.title: Fourth engine started
events.detail: The crew started engine 3 during taxi and completed the delayed-start checks.
events.caption: The crew started the remaining engine while taxiing and completed the checks.

events.title: Cleared onto departure runway
events.detail: ATC cleared the aircraft to position and hold on runway 22R, with a wake-turbulence caution for a Boeing 757.
events.caption: Controllers cleared the aircraft onto the runway to wait, warning of disturbed air behind a Boeing 757.

events.title: Takeoff clearance
events.detail: ATC cleared takeoff on runway 22R and reported wind from 240° at 8 knots. The statement is a tower report; it is not the offshore wind.
events.caption: Controllers cleared the aircraft for takeoff from runway 22R.

events.title: Aircraft becomes airborne
events.detail: FDR and CVR place liftoff at about 20:19 EDT. This timestamp is rounded, not an exact wheel-off measurement.
events.caption: The aircraft lifted off at about 8:19 p.m. local time.

events.title: Departure control contacted
events.detail: The crew contacted Kennedy departure control during the initial climb.
events.caption: The crew contacted departure control as the aircraft began climbing.

events.title: Handoff to Boston Center
events.detail: The crew was transferred to Boston Center as the climb continued.
events.caption: Boston Center took over air traffic control as the aircraft continued climbing.

events.title: Higher altitude assigned
events.detail: Boston Center instructed a climb to 19,000 ft and expedited passage through 15,000 ft. The crew acknowledged.
events.caption: Controllers cleared a climb to 19,000 feet, asking the crew to pass through 15,000 feet quickly.

events.title: Clearance amended to thirteen thousand
events.detail: ATC amended the clearance to maintain 13,000 ft MSL.
events.caption: Controllers changed the clearance, instructing the crew to maintain 13,000 feet.

events.title: Altitude alert sounds
events.detail: The CVR recorded an altitude alert. FDR data showed the aircraft reaching its assigned altitude.
events.caption: An altitude alert sounded as the aircraft reached its assigned height.

events.title: Fuel flow reading questioned
events.detail: The captain drew attention to an unusual engine 4 fuel-flow indication. This did not establish the later ignition mechanism.
events.quote: Look at that crazy fuel flow indicator there on number four
events.locator: AAR section 1.1 p. 2; official CVR transcript 2029:15
events.caption: The captain noticed an unusual fuel flow reading. Its connection to the later ignition was not established.

events.title: Climb to fifteen thousand cleared
events.detail: Boston Center cleared a climb to 15,000 ft MSL. The crew called for climb thrust.
events.caption: Controllers cleared a climb to 15,000 feet. The crew called for more engine power.

events.title: Last radio acknowledgment
events.detail: The right-seat captain/check airman acknowledged the climb clearance. The CVR clock gives 20:30:19.2; Boston Center gives 20:30:19.4 after correlation.
events.locator: CVR factual narrative p. 4; s2 time-correlation table printed p. 6
events.caption: The captain in the right seat acknowledged the climb clearance. This was the last radio acknowledgment.

events.title: Climb power set
events.detail: The flight engineer reported the power setting complete. Recorded engine EPR subsequently rose as the aircraft climbed.
events.locator: AAR section 1.1 p. 2; revised FDR Attachment II pp. 40–41
events.caption: The flight engineer confirmed the power setting. Engine power then rose as the aircraft climbed.

events.title: Last Islip secondary return
events.detail: The final Islip entry in the witness radar table reported X 19.5121 nm east and Y 8.6881 nm south of its antenna. Its altitude code was 137. Other radar sites continued briefly.
events.locator: Attachment C p. 4/62 (PDF p. 14), TWA800 last row
events.caption: Islip radar received its last aircraft reply. Other radar sites continued tracking it briefly.

events.title: Last FDR data word
events.detail: The revised recorder analysis places the last recorded data word here. The investigators bounded power loss between this time and 00:31:12.89 UTC; the table must not be extended with the previous flight's data.
events.locator: s2 printed pp. 6–7; s3 discussion and corrected final table
events.caption: The flight recorder stopped recording data. The exact moment it lost power is uncertain.

events.title: Last transponder return
events.detail: The last secondary return across the radar sources was recorded by the Trevose site at about 20:31:12 EDT. Subsequent primary echoes lacked transponder identity and altitude.
events.caption: Radar received the aircraft's last identifying reply. Later echoes carried no aircraft identity or altitude.

events.title: Center wing tank explodes
events.detail: The NTSB placed the initiating explosion in the center wing tank. This is a physical-evidence finding timed to recorder termination, not a recorder measurement of ignition or internal pressure.
events.caption: An explosion in the fuel tank between the wings began the breakup. The exact ignition time is unknown.

events.title: Cockpit recording ends
events.detail: A loud transient lasting about 0.117 second preceded loss of the CVR recording. Brief changes in electrical background noise on the captain's channel occurred within the last second; they do not uniquely identify the ignition fault.
events.locator: AAR sections 1.1 p. 3, 1.11.1–1.11.1.1; s2 printed p. 6
events.caption: A brief, loud sound preceded the end of the cockpit recording.

events.title: Forward fuselage separates
events.detail: Published NTSB models place nose separation about 3–5 seconds after the initial event. This range would fall near 00:31:15–17 UTC, but no exact separation instant was recorded.
events.locator: Dennis Crider Main Wreckage Flight Path Study and addenda; AAR p. 263 footnote 550
events.caption: The nose is estimated to have separated about three to five seconds after the initial explosion.

events.title: Main body pitches upward
events.detail: NTSB simulations show the remaining aircraft briefly climbing and changing direction after losing the nose. Altitude, attitude and timing after the cutoff are model outputs, with several acceptable trajectories.
events.caption: The remaining aircraft is estimated to have briefly climbed and changed direction after losing its nose.

events.title: Outboard wings separate in model
events.detail: The final NTSB timing model assumes outboard wing failure 34 seconds after the initial event. This was inferred from wreckage, witnesses and modelling; it was not a recorded failure time.
events.locator: Dennis Crider Addendum II, printed pp. 2–3; AAR table 4 p. 97, p. 263
events.caption: The outer wings are estimated to have failed about 34 seconds after the initial explosion.

events.title: Nearby pilot reports explosion
events.detail: The captain of Eastwind flight 507 reported seeing an explosion. This is the radio report time, not a reliable timestamp for the initial tank explosion.
events.caption: A nearby airline captain reported seeing an explosion. The report does not establish when the initial explosion happened.

events.title: Center section fails in model
events.detail: The final model assumes center-section failure adjacent to the left wing 38 seconds after the initial event. The resulting pieces follow ballistic paths rather than a controllable aircraft trajectory.
events.locator: Dennis Crider Addendum II printed pp. 2–3; AAR table 4 p. 97
events.caption: The center section is estimated to have failed near the left wing, leaving pieces falling without control.

events.title: Main wreckage reaches the ocean
events.detail: The NTSB estimated 47–54 seconds from the initiating explosion to main-body water impact, approximately 00:31:59–00:32:06 UTC. The forward fuselage impacted separately; no single exact time or point is established for all wreckage.
events.caption: The main wreckage hit the ocean an estimated 47–54 seconds after the explosion. The nose fell separately.

events.title: Search and recovery begin
events.detail: On the evening of 17 July local time, aircraft and boats responded to the burning wreckage. No survivors were found.
events.locator: Sections 1.12 and 1.15; appendix A investigation/recovery history
events.caption: Aircraft and boats responded to the burning wreckage that evening. No survivors were found.

events.title: Recorders recovered
events.detail: Both recorders were recovered on 24 July 1996. The FDR arrived at the NTSB laboratory early on 25 July and yielded readable tape. Exact recovery UTC times are not supplied here.
events.locator: s2 summary printed p. 2; s6 recorder recovery narrative
events.caption: Both recorders were recovered on July 24. The flight recorder's tape was readable.

events.title: FBI ends active criminal investigation
events.detail: On 18 November 1997, the FBI announced no evidence of a criminal cause and withdrew from active involvement. The CIA animation presented in that context was a reconstruction of possible witness perceptions.
events.locator: AAR appendix A and sections 1.18.4–2.2.2; Appendix FF CIA briefing
events.caption: The FBI ended its active criminal investigation, announcing it had found no evidence of a criminal cause.

events.title: NTSB adopts probable cause
events.detail: On 23 August 2000, the NTSB adopted its tank-explosion finding. It identified excessive voltage through fuel-quantity wiring as the most likely ignition route, while leaving the actual source uncertain.
events.caption: Investigators found a tank explosion, probably ignited by excessive voltage through fuel gauge wiring. The source remains uncertain.

events.title: Petition seeks reconsideration
events.detail: On 19 June 2013, the TWA 800 Project submitted radar, witness and physical-evidence arguments challenging the NTSB findings. Some petitioners had participated in the original investigation; the submission was not an official Board dissent.
events.locator: Cover letter and petition introductory statement
events.caption: Petitioners challenged the findings using radar, witness accounts, and physical evidence. Some had participated in the original investigation.

events.title: Petitioners present their case
events.detail: On 10 January 2014, NTSB staff heard the petitioners' presentation, including an eyewitness. The meeting was a listening session for the petition, not adoption of a new cause.
events.caption: Investigators heard the petitioners' case, including an eyewitness account. The meeting did not establish a new cause.

events.title: NTSB denies the petition
events.detail: On 2 July 2014, the NTSB denied reconsideration in full after reviewing the radar arguments and 20 additional interview summaries. It also answered physical-evidence and process allegations in an attachment.
events.caption: Investigators rejected the request to reconsider after reviewing radar arguments and additional witness accounts.

events.title: Reconstruction retirement announced
events.detail: On 22 February 2021, the NTSB announced retirement of its physical reconstruction from training use and plans for 3D documentation. It said the wreckage would be destroyed in keeping with its agreement with families.
events.locator: 22 February 2021 release; announced cessation date 7 July 2021
events.caption: Investigators announced plans to retire the reconstructed wreckage and document it digitally before destruction, as agreed with families.

events.title: Renewed records advocacy in 2026
events.detail: On 18 July 2026, Judicial Watch announced a documentary and receipt of FBI records. The opened extract records early leads and faxes claiming responsibility; it does not verify an attack or replace the technical investigation.
events.locator: s23 release dated 18 July 2026; s24 PDF pp. 1–4
events.caption: Judicial Watch announced FBI records describing early leads and claims of responsibility. These did not verify an attack.

events.title: New archive finding aid published
events.detail: The Clinton Library finding aid updated on 28 August 2026 describes newly processed TWA 800 records. It is an archival development; no new NTSB probable-cause determination was found in the 2024–2026 search through 7 November 2026.
events.locator: s22 extent, scope and last-modified fields; current NTSB case and 2014 decision
events.caption: The Clinton Library announced newly processed records. No new official cause determination was identified.

perspectives.label: Center tank explosion
perspectives.held_by: NTSB Board, supported by its structures, fire/explosion and performance work
perspectives.claim: A flammable fuel/air mixture exploded in the center wing tank and initiated structural breakup. Excess voltage entering through fuel-quantity indication wiring was the most likely ignition route considered, but the actual initiating fault was not established.

evidence_for.text: Tank fracture/deformation and soot patterns, together with early tank and adjacent debris, support overpressure originating in the CWT. The Fire and Explosion group found no initiating fire beneath it.
Thermal testing and combustion research showed that Jet A vapor in the nearly empty, heated tank could be flammable under accident conditions.
No corroborating missile penetration or high-order detonation damage was identified in the recovered structure.

evidence_against.text: The specific short, entry point, ignition energy and ignition location remain uncertain; the wiring hypothesis is a most-likely explanation, not a recovered failed-circuit proof.

The witness group acknowledged 38 near-vertical streak descriptions that seemed inconsistent with its calculated aircraft path; the Board nevertheless found the whole record favored the aircraft-fire explanation.

ending.description: The nose separates first. NTSB models then have the remaining aircraft pitch up, turn and descend before later wing/center-section failure. The estimated 47–54 second sequence and approximate 15,000–16,000 ft peak are model results, not recorded flight data. No exact post-cutoff coordinate series is supplied.

perspectives.label: External explosion or missile
perspectives.held_by: TWA 800 Project petitioners, including some former investigation participants; other missile-theory advocates
perspectives.claim: The petitioners argue that radar debris motion, rising-light accounts, fractures and residue point to an external high-velocity explosion. A missile is a proposed mechanism among advocates; the petition did not establish a unique launch site, weapon, perpetrator or reproducible flight path.

evidence_for.text: Some witness descriptions depict a light apparently rising from the surface; the NTSB witness group itself documented an inconsistent subset rather than dismissing every account as a perfect fit.
Trace explosives were genuinely detected on three recovered pieces. Petitioners interpret residues and certain fractures as support for an energetic external cause.
The petition offers two radar analyses and 20 additional FBI interview summaries as reasons to reconsider.

evidence_against.text: Primary returns cannot reliably be assigned to the same fragment on successive sweeps. Resolution, cross-site offsets and secondary-to-primary discontinuity invalidate the claimed precise sideways debris velocities.
The physical examinations found no associated missile penetration or high-order blast damage; residue alone did not establish detonation, and its origin remains unknown.
NTSB review of the 20 summaries found eight ascending-light accounts, three mentioning surface/horizon origin, with no unique new vantage point. The Board denied the petition on 2 July 2014.

The NTSB review of military records found no military surface vessels within 15 nm. The unidentified roughly 30-knot surface track was not identified as a military vessel; lack of its identity does not establish a launch.

ending.description: An external detonation would precede or initiate the observed breakup. No verified alternative final path, exact attack time, launch position or impact point was established; no invented missile track is included.

perspectives.label: Onboard bomb
perspectives.held_by: FBI and NTSB as an early investigative possibility; later terrorism advocates
perspectives.claim: A bomb inside the aircraft was investigated as a possible trigger for the sudden breakup. Early responsibility claims and trace residues were leads, not a demonstrated causal chain.

evidence_for.text: FBI testing detected trace explosive compounds on two floor-panel pieces and a canvas-like piece.
An early FBI communication, released in the 2026 FOIA extract, records faxes from Cairo claiming responsibility. The extract does not authenticate them.

evidence_against.text: Recovered structure, furnishings and seats lacked the high-energy damage expected from an onboard bomb. The tank-overpressure sequence explained the early debris distribution.
The 2026 extract is an incomplete early investigative communication, not a later forensic finding or confirmation of responsibility.

ending.description: A bomb theory changes the initiating source rather than supplying a substantiated different route. No evidence-backed alternative track or separate exact ending is available.

perspectives.label: CIA witness reconstruction
perspectives.held_by: CIA analysts assisting the FBI; publicly presented in November 1997
perspectives.claim: CIA analysts built an independent model to explain how burning aircraft wreckage could appear as a rising streak. Its animation was an interpretation of witness perception and estimated aircraft motion; it was not the NTSB's definitive measured trajectory.

evidence_for.text: CIA analysts and NTSB independently obtained a brief post-nose-loss climb, although their assumptions and paths differed. The released briefing discusses these differences.
Sound-travel delay and the timing of visible later fireballs can explain why many witnesses first noticed events after the initial tank explosion.

evidence_against.text: The 1999 briefing records challenges to engine-power, bank and climb assumptions. The 3,000-ft climb discussed for the CIA video must not be substituted for a recorder measurement or for the later NTSB model family.
Nose-off aerodynamics and the primary radar position/identity uncertainties prevent a unique precise reconstruction.

ending.description: The CIA animation uses its own pitch-up/climb and breakup depiction. Its path is not imported as the baseline track; the NTSB model family and the animation are distinguished. No numerical alternate curve has been transcribed.

evidence_points.label: Last Islip secondary position
evidence_points.detail: Coordinates calculated from published X/Y using the method in the matching radar track point. This is the identified aircraft before the breakup, not the main-body impact point.

evidence_points.label: Islip radar antenna
evidence_points.detail: Antenna reference position 40°47′38.2″N, 73°06′00.5″W in Attachment A; decimal conversion. Origin for the published X/Y radar table.

evidence_points.label: Approximate accident reference
evidence_points.detail: Position used for the NTSB meteorology group astronomical calculations. It represents the general area only, not an identified piece of wreckage or an exact point of impact.

evidence_points.label: Red debris zone
evidence_points.detail: AAR figure 22a and section 1.12.1, pp. 66, 69: western/largest zone. Included CWT/front-spar pieces, structure beneath and just forward of the tank, floor beams and air-conditioning packs. These early-separated pieces generally had little soot or fire evidence. Zone polygon and centroid are not numerically transcribed.

evidence_points.label: Yellow debris zone
evidence_points.detail: AAR section 1.12.2 p. 70: smallest zone, within the northeast of the red zone. Predominantly forward fuselage and nose; severe water-impact crushing, no soot/fire/heat evidence. Zone is an area, not one impact point.

evidence_points.label: Green debris zone
evidence_points.detail: AAR section 1.12.3: farther east, containing most of the wings, aft fuselage and empennage. Much of the principal aircraft mass travelled farther than the nose. Some fire damage may include fire on the water. Exact polygon not transcribed.

evidence_points.label: Physical reconstruction at Calverton
evidence_points.detail: AAR section 1.16.3 describes the 93-ft-long central fuselage reconstruction and smaller component layouts. Its later training use and planned 3D archiving are documented by the NTSB. Exact hangar coordinates were not verified.

witnesses.said: Paraphrase of official ATC and NTSB interview characterisation: saw an explosion and burning material descending ahead, then reported it at 20:31:50 EDT. The NTSB says he did not see a missile or anything rise toward or strike the aircraft. His radio report time does not establish initial explosion time.

Paraphrase of NTSB characterisation: described a flare and later explosion/fireball. The NTSB reconstructed the view and determined TWA 800 was outside this passenger's field of view at the initiating explosion; it interpreted the later flare as burning aircraft fuel. Exact observer coordinates are not transcribed.

witnesses.who: Air National Guard helicopter crew near the coast
witnesses.said: Paraphrase of NTSB characterisation: crew members described a streak, explosions and descending fire. The investigation compared their view with timing and sound propagation; not every member had the same initial view. Private identities and speculative exact observation coordinates are omitted.

witnesses.who: Witness group subset describing near-vertical streaks
witnesses.said: Paraphrase of Witness Group Study conclusions: 38 accounts described a streak rising straight up or nearly so, which seemed inconsistent with the calculated aircraft path. The group cautioned that interview summaries and eyewitness accounts alone cannot prove a cause.

witnesses.who: Shore-based witness in an early FBI lead
witnesses.said: Paraphrase of the 19 July 1996 FBI communication released in 2026: a walker described an object resembling fireworks rising, followed by a puff and descending fireball, and showed agents a suspected origin location. This extract reports a lead under investigation, not a confirmed launch site.

numbers.label: Vertical streak accounts challenging estimated path

why_it_matters: The investigation drove fuel-tank ignition-prevention and wiring safety rules, followed by requirements to reduce flammable fuel-tank exposure, including inerting where applicable. It also helped establish stronger family-assistance arrangements and clearer FBI–NTSB investigation coordination. Sources: s16 (decision p. 11), s19 (rulemaking), s21 (family assistance and coordination).

conflicts.a: Missile advocates interpret some upward or surface-origin streak descriptions as a weapon approaching the aircraft.
conflicts.b: The Board interprets most as burning fuel after the tank explosion. The witness group nonetheless recorded 38 near-vertical accounts apparently inconsistent with its computed path and limitations in the FBI summaries.

conflicts.a: The petition argues that primary echoes show rapidly sideways-projected debris incompatible with the official cause.
conflicts.b: NTSB says scatter, resolution, secondary/primary offsets and inability to identify a continuous fragment track invalidate those speed calculations.

conflicts.a: Petitioners alleged approximately 100 or more explosive detections and challenged a dog-training contamination explanation.
conflicts.b: The 2014 response identifies three positive pieces and no right-wing positive result or blast damage. It confirms that a training exercise occurred but explicitly does not establish it as the residue source; recovery contamination was another possibility.

conflicts.a: Judicial Watch's July 2026 advocacy release uses 755 reports, 183 streak descriptions and 96 surface-origin descriptions.
conflicts.b: The NTSB final analysed witness population is 736, with 258 streak witnesses and 25 surface/horizon origins among those streak witnesses. These are different classifications/populations and must not be merged as equivalent counts.

conflicts.about: Early radar attack lead versus final analysis
conflicts.a: The 19 July 1996 FBI extract mentions an unidentified object rapidly approaching, with FAA specialist review pending.
conflicts.b: The final NTSB analysis found no radar sequence intersecting the aircraft and rejected attack interpretation of the anomalous tracks. The extract lacks the preceding context and final disposition of that individual early lead.

conflicts.a: The 1996 FBI communication gives approximately 20:35 local time.
conflicts.b: Synchronised CVR/FDR and radar place recorder termination at about 20:31:12 EDT; the early rounded FBI lead time is not used for playback.

conflicts.a: CIA visualisation and early NTSB simulations used different bank, engine-power and breakup assumptions. Early model timing also contains a corrected clock-time error.
conflicts.b: The NTSB addenda and final report present a family of uncertain paths with revised wing-failure assumptions. None is recorded flight data; no unique peak altitude or exact attitude history is established.

conflicts.a: The original table's lined-through final values were interpreted by some reviewers as anomalous Flight 800 motion.
conflicts.b: The revised analysis shows those old data came from the previously recorded TWA803 flight. They are excluded here; the revised table ends Flight 800 data at 20:31:12.

conflicts.about: Raw recorder anomalies versus physical motion
conflicts.a: The revised table contains an isolated IAS 455 kt at 20:30:21 and smaller raw altitude/heading irregularities.
conflicts.b: The FDR specialist documents occasional anomalous IAS and other parameters. These raw values are preserved and flagged, not silently treated as genuine aircraft acceleration or turn rate.

conflicts.a: AAR p. 6 describes a 747-100 as about 225 ft long. Boeing section 2.2.1 labels overall length 231 ft 10 in, alongside an inconsistent 70.4 m conversion.
conflicts.b: This JSON uses the explicit manufacturer imperial overall dimension, converted by 0.3048 m/ft to 70.66 m. The shorter AAR description is not substituted for overall geometry.

conflicts.a: The current FAA lesson broadly says no bomb/missile fragments, explosive residue or other evidence were found.
conflicts.b: The NTSB original report and 2014 response explicitly document trace explosive residues on three pieces while rejecting a bomb/missile cause. This JSON follows those detailed primary findings.

conflicts.a: AAR section 1.6 p. 6 says the aircraft was manufactured in July 1971 and entered the TWA operating certificate on 27 October 1971.
conflicts.b: The current FAA lesson says manufactured in November 1971. This JSON does not assert a manufacture month; the detailed accident report and FAA summary disagree.

conflicts.about: Clock alignment is not subsecond certainty
conflicts.a: The CVR transcription places the last radio acknowledgment at 20:30:19.2 and the Boston Center correlation table at 20:30:19.4.
conflicts.b: The FDR report says correlation points agree within one second. Exact decimals refer to their own correlated time bases and are not a claim that every event is timed to a hundredth of a second.

unknowns: The exact electrical fault, point of entry into the CWT, ignition location and ignition energy were not established; fuel-quantity wiring is the NTSB's most-likely route, not certainty.

No FDR/CVR data exist after power loss. Exact nose separation time, main-body pitch/roll, engine thrust, peak altitude and final water-impact time are not measured. Published post-cutoff model curves were read but no reliable numerical ordinate series was transcribed.

The 150 track points are 78 radar position observations and 72 revised one-second FDR row samples. They are separate observations, not 150 complete aircraft states. The FDR had no positional parameters; no coordinates were invented for its samples and no interpolation was baked into this file.

All 72 FDR rows use first listed parameter values within the second; the underlying system samples asynchronously at roughly 0.671875-second frame intervals. Exact subsecond time of each selected value is not recoverable from the labelled printed row alone.
Some raw recorder values are anomalous. In particular IAS 455 kt at 00:30:21 UTC should not drive physical motion. No unsupported filter or corrected replacement number is supplied.

The original NTSB X/Y-to-geographic projection and geographic datum were not fully specified in the radar table. The WGS84 local inverse used here is approximate. Radar coordinates rounded to 0.0001° do not imply that precision of measurement; cross-site offsets can be much larger.

The published Islip altitude codes are retained in radar method strings, but their absolute MSL correction was not verified. Radar alt_ft is therefore null. FDR altitude is the NTSB's already-corrected MSL value; no second correction is applied.

No exact individual final debris-impact positions, red/yellow/green polygons or defensible zone centroids were transcribed from the chart database. Their evidence-point coordinates are null. The three zones are areas; they must not be displayed as precise point impacts.

Water depth at each debris zone and accident-site sea state/wave height were not established from the opened accident sources. NOAA buoy 44025 supplies actual regional wave observations, but its 1996 mooring position was not verified and its measurements cannot be assigned to the accident site.

Cloud type and cloud tops for the surface station layers are unknown. GOES only constrains nearby top heights, not the same cloud parcels. Surface bases have been converted from AGL with current field elevations and must not be treated as precise 1996 aircraft-level clouds.
No reliable local turbulence measurement was found. Lightning networks had incomplete offshore/all-flash coverage, so absence of detected local lightning is not coded as an absolute false.

The full planned navigation waypoint list was not found in the opened final report and dispatch-release packet. Current airport reference coordinates are from a secondary dataset, not historical runway/gate coordinates.

Accident-specific geometric height, numeric wing sweep and exact paint details on 17 July 1996 were not verified. Reference dimensions are used; wing_sweep_deg is null. The FAA-hosted N93119 photograph is undated.
The precise source and deposition date of the three explosive residues remain unknown. A dog-training exercise and recovery handling are possibilities, not proved explanations for every detection.
The anonymous 30-knot surface radar track was not positively identified. Lack of identity is not proof of a missile boat; the reviewed record contains no verified weapon launch or attacker.

Individual witness observation coordinates and exact observation times are not transcribed here. Accounts are carefully marked as paraphrases; original FBI documents are often unreviewed interview summaries rather than verbatim witness transcripts.

Most investigation/petition/recovery milestones have dates but no verified UTC clock time. Their t_utc is null and the date is stated in the detail rather than inventing midnight. Null-timed breakup events carry explicit estimated time ranges.

The 2024–2026 search found renewed FOIA advocacy, a 2026 FBI extract and a newly processed Clinton Library collection, but no new official probable-cause determination. The full 415-page FOIA production and approximately 1,900-page archive collection were not read; their uninspected contents and any still-pending legal outcome remain unknown.
memorial_note: All 212 passengers and 18 crew members aboard TWA Flight 800 lost their lives; this reconstruction is made in their memory.

sources.title: In-flight Breakup Over the Atlantic Ocean, TWA Flight 800, NTSB/AAR-00/03
sources.notes: Adopted 23 August 2000. Downloaded with curl; all 341 PDF pages extracted locally with PyMuPDF. Printed page numbers are 18 lower than PDF page numbers in the main report. Sections 1.1, 1.6, 1.7, 1.12, 1.16, 1.18, 2.2 and conclusions consulted. All local flight times are EDT (section 1.1 footnote 1); add four hours and change date to 18 July for times after 20:00 EDT. Meteorology source s5 independently specifies EDT = UTC minus four hours. Report summary altitude is rounded; track uses revised recorder table values.

sources.title: Flight Data Recorder Group Chairman Factual Report, Revision 1, Exhibit 10A
sources.notes: Dated 15 February 2000. Downloaded and text extracted; scanned tables on PDF pages 40–43 visually read. Attachment II, Tabular Data No. 1, revised 22 December 1999. Track takes the first listed value of each selected parameter in each labelled second, without averaging or interpolation. Multiple samples within a second and different parameter sampling phases are not simultaneous. Printed MSL altitude already incorporates the investigators' 127 ft pressure-altitude correction (printed p. 6); do not add it again. Heading is magnetic, roll is signed as printed. This table has acknowledged raw parameter anomalies. FDR contains no latitude/longitude. The document header says local standard time, but its summary, correlation table and s5 establish EDT.

sources.title: Flight Data Recorder Group Chairman Factual Report, Addendum 2
sources.notes: Dated 15 February 2000. Downloaded and read. Explains erase/write-head geometry and why lined-through post-cutoff values in the original report were from TWA803, not TWA800. Revised final page excludes those values. Last Flight 800 data word is at 20:31:11.96 EDT; power loss window is 20:31:11.96–12.89 EDT in s2, printed pp. 6–7.

sources.title: Witness Group Recorded Radar Study
sources.notes: Dated 17 June 1999. Downloaded and extracted; Attachment A geographic references and Attachment C scanned tables visually read after rotating pages. Attachment C pp. 1–4 (PDF pp. 11–14) lists TWA800 Islip secondary returns in UTC, X true east/Y true north in nautical miles from ISP ASR; altitude column is in hundreds of feet. The erroneous 2045 accident-time cover entry is not used. Geographic coordinates in this JSON are an explicitly approximate inverse local projection of these recorded positions, not coordinates printed in the table. The last Islip return at 00:31:11.52 is earlier than the last return from all radar sites.

sources.title: Meteorology Group Chairman Factual Report, Exhibit 5A
sources.notes: Dated 18 June 1997. Downloaded and read. Printed pp. 1–3 surface observations and units; pp. 3–4 Upton sounding; pp. 5–7 lightning, satellite and weather radar; pp. 8–9 astronomy. Surface cloud heights are AGL; other heights MSL. UTC is used except where explicitly marked EDT. Source gives station temperatures directly in Celsius. Sea state and wave heights are not supplied.

sources.title: Cockpit Voice Recorder Group Chairman Factual Report, Exhibit 12A
sources.notes: Downloaded and read the factual narrative and relevant transcript pages. Official transcript only; no audio reproduced. Printed p. 4 summarises pushback, engine starts, takeoff clearance and last transmission. Final local transcript time is 2031:12.5. The last acknowledgment begins at 2030:19.2 in this CVR transcription, versus Boston Center time 2030:19.4 in s2; these are distinct correlated clocks, not exact universal timing.

sources.title: Airplane Performance Study, Exhibit 13A
sources.notes: Dated 30 September 1997. Downloaded and read, especially printed pp. 2–7 and time-correlation table. Describes radar sources, site alignment, secondary/primary limitations and unexplained surface track. NY Center time offset −2.25 s and NY TRACON −0.25 s apply to that study's original data correlation; they have not been applied again to s4's published UTC table.

sources.title: Witness Group Study Report
sources.notes: Dated 9 February 2000. Downloaded and read, especially pp. 5–25 and 42–45. Counts refer to the report's classified witness population; FBI interview documents are summaries, generally not witness-checked verbatim accounts. All group members agreed that eyewitness accounts alone cannot establish or exclude a cause; 38 near-vertical streak accounts seemed inconsistent with the calculated aircraft path.

sources.title: Fire and Explosion Group Factual Report, Exhibit 20A
sources.notes: Dated 31 October 1997. Downloaded and read, particularly printed pp. 2 and 4–9 and findings on physical damage. Overpressure evidence in CWT, soot distribution and absence of high-order explosive damage. No ignition source confirmed by that group at that stage. Contains descriptive component examination records; does not give a measured post-explosion flight path.

sources.title: Main Wreckage Flight Path Study, Exhibit 22C
sources.notes: Dennis Crider, 21 November 1997. Downloaded and read. Published simulation, not FDR data. Engine-power alternatives; estimated nose-off aerodynamics; bank and pitching moment adjusted to match radar and wreckage constraints. Initial assumptions of fireball and impact timing were later revised. Read with errata s11 and addenda s12/s13.

sources.title: Errata Main Wreckage Flight Path Study, Exhibit 22D
sources.notes: Dennis Crider, 4 December 1997. Both PDF pages opened and read. Corrects one model's nose-departure clock time from 20:31:13.4 to 20:31:15.2 and wing-tip failure from 20:31:51.4 to 20:31:53.2. These are model timing corrections, not independently timed observations; s13 subsequently examines other wing-failure timing.

sources.title: Addendum 1 to Main Wreckage Flight Path Study
sources.notes: Dennis Crider, 11 February 2000. Downloaded and read. Quantifies radar range/azimuth resolution and multiple plausible fitted trajectories. Reports FAA range accuracy ±1/16 nautical mile; cross-site secondary tracks form a roughly 1/4–1/2 nautical-mile band. Assumed 10,000 ft altitude solely to convert primary-return slant range, not a measured primary altitude.

sources.title: Addendum II to Main Wreckage Flight Path Study, Exhibit 22F
sources.notes: Dennis Crider, 9 June 2000. Downloaded and read. Explores outboard wing failure 34 s and center-section failure 38 s after initial event. Nose-off uncertainty approximately 3–5 s. Fast simulations with different radar sets show a family of solutions; aerodynamic characteristics without the nose or outer panels cannot be modelled precisely. No numerical curve points digitized into this JSON.

sources.title: Summary and Conclusions of Explosion Research Team, Exhibit 20W
sources.notes: Dated 1 August 2000. Downloaded and read. Documents Jet A flammability experiments, thermal measurements, quarter-scale tests and two numerical combustion methods. Research supports a flammable CWT and fuel/air deflagration; uncertainty prevented a unique ignition location. This is a primary technical submission, not an independently peer-reviewed article.

sources.title: Petition for Reconsideration and Modification of Findings and Probable Cause
sources.notes: Submitted 19 June 2013 by Henry F. Hughes, Thomas F. Stalcup and other petitioners, including some former investigation participants and relatives. Downloaded and read petition arguments and radar/witness analyses. The NTSB hosts it as an official docket filing; its causal claims remain those of the petitioners, not NTSB findings.

sources.title: Response to Petition for Reconsideration
sources.notes: Dated 2 July 2014. All 24 PDF pages downloaded and read. Decision pp. 1–11; attachment separately numbered pp. 1–13. Rejects petition in entirety. Discusses radar resolution, 20 additional interview summaries, spike-tooth fractures, explosive residues, reconstruction database, institutional process and models. Locators specify PDF page when useful.

sources.title: Correspondence from CIA and Transcript of CIA Briefing to Witness Group, Appendix FF
sources.notes: Cover letter 12 January 2000 releases transcript of 30 April 1999 briefing. Downloaded and read relevant passages on FBI assistance, timing of witness observations and independent CIA/NTSB simulations, including transcript pp. 65–68. The 1997 animation is an explanatory reconstruction, not camera footage, radar altitude, or a measured trajectory.

sources.title: 747 Airplane Characteristics for Airport Planning, D6-58326

sources.notes: Opened current FAA accident lesson, rulemaking discussion and linked photograph of N93119.
